title: Git, GitHub, and Developer Workflow
summary: Version control is a non-negotiable skill for any engineer. Git tracks every change to your code so you can experiment safely, revert mistakes, and collaborate without overwriting others' work. GitHub hosts your repositories and is also your public p
content:
# Git, GitHub, and Developer Workflow ##### The experiment that erased four days of work A student was training a text classifier. Accuracy sat at 82%. Over four days they tried a dozen changes — different features, a new preprocessing step, tuned hyperparameters — and got it to 91%. Then they tried a "quick improvement," rewrote the preprocessing function, and accuracy dropped to 74%. They tried to undo it. But they had been editing one file in place, saving over it each time. There was no previous version. The 91% configuration existed only in a screenshot of a terminal, and they could not reconstruct which combination of changes had produced it. Four days of work, gone, because there was no record of *how* the code had changed. **Git** exists for exactly this. It records every version of every file with a message explaining why it changed, lets you return to any point in history, and lets you experiment on a branch without touching what already works. For an AI engineer specifically, that last property is decisive: your job involves constant experimentation, and experimentation without the ability to revert is gambling. ##### The mental model Git tracks **snapshots**. Each snapshot — a **commit** — records the state of your files plus a message, an author and a timestamp. Commits form a chain you can navigate. Files move through four states: ```text working directory → staging area → local repository → remote (GitHub) (you edit) (git add) (git commit) (git push) ``` The **staging area** exists so you can commit some changes and not others. If you fixed a bug and started an unrelated experiment in the same session, you can commit just the fix. ##### Setup and the daily loop Configure Git once per machine: ```bash git config --global user.name "Ananya Rao" git config --global user.email "ananya@example.com" git config --global init.defaultBranch main ``` Then, per project: ```bash mkdir churn-predictor && cd churn-predictor git init # Create .gitignore FIRST — before any secret or large file exists cat > .gitignore <<'EOF' .venv/ __pycache__/ *.pyc .env .ipynb_checkpoints/ data/raw/ *.csv *.pkl *.pt *.h5 models/ EOF git add .gitignore git commit -m "chore: add gitignore for Python and ML artefacts" ``` That `.gitignore` is worth studying, because AI projects have specific hazards. **`.env`** holds API keys. **`data/`** and `*.csv` are usually too large and often contain personal data. **`*.pkl`, `*.pt`, `*.h5`** are model weights — frequently hundreds of megabytes, and Git handles large binaries badly. **`.ipynb_checkpoints/`** is Jupyter's autosave clutter. The daily loop: ```bash git status # what changed? — run this constantly git diff # exactly what changed, line by line git add train.py # stage one file git add . # stage everything (check status first!) git commit -m "feat: add TF-IDF preprocessing, accuracy 0.82 -> 0.87" git log --oneline --graph # readable history ``` **Commit messages matter, and for ML work they should record results.** Compare: ```text update ← useless feat: add TF-IDF preprocessing, acc 0.82 -> 0.87 ← tells you what and how much fix: stratify train/test split, was leaking classes exp: try n_estimators=500 (no improvement, reverted) docs: document data cleaning assumptions ``` Six months later, `git log --oneline` becomes a searchable record of every experiment and its outcome. That alone would have saved the student in the opening story. ##### Undoing things This is why Git is worth the learning curve: ```bash git restore train.py # discard uncommitted changes to a file git restore --staged train.py # unstage but keep the changes git commit --amend -m "better msg" # fix the most recent commit message git revert a1b2c3d # new commit that undoes an old one (safe) git checkout a1b2c3d -- train.py # recover one file from an old commit git reset --hard a1b2c3d # DANGEROUS: discards everything after ``` Prefer `git revert` over `git reset --hard` on anything you have shared. Revert adds a new commit undoing the change, preserving history; reset rewrites it, which breaks things for anyone who has pulled. ##### Branching and merging A **branch** is an independent line of development. This is the feature that makes safe experimentation possible. ```bash git switch -c experiment/word-embeddings # create and switch # ... edit, run, commit as usual ... git switch main # back to the working version git merge experiment/word-embeddings # bring the work in git branch -d experiment/word-embeddings # tidy up ``` ```mermaid gitGraph commit id: "init" commit id: "baseline 0.82" branch experiment/tfidf commit id: "add TF-IDF" commit id: "tune params 0.87" checkout main commit id: "fix data loader" merge experiment/tfidf commit id: "v1: acc 0.87" ``` For AI work the pattern is: **`main` holds your best working version; each experiment gets a branch.** If the experiment improves things, merge it. If it does not, delete the branch — and `main` was never touched. The 91% configuration would have been a commit on `main`, permanently recoverable. A useful convention for branch names: `experiment/`, `feature/`, `fix/`, `docs/`. **Merge conflicts** occur when two branches change the same lines. Git marks them in the file: ```text <<<<<<< HEAD learning_rate = 0.001 ======= learning_rate = 0.01 >>>>>>> experiment/tuning ``` Edit the file to the version you want, delete the three marker lines, then `git add` and `git commit`. Conflicts feel alarming the first time and become routine by the fifth. A tip specific to this field: **notebooks conflict horribly** because their JSON includes output and execution counts. Keep serious code in `.py` files and use notebooks for exploration. ##### GitHub and remote repositories GitHub hosts your repository remotely — a backup, a collaboration surface, and for someone building a career, a portfolio. ```bash gh repo create churn-predictor --public --source=. --push # or manually: git remote add origin https://github.com//churn-predictor.git git push -u origin main ``` Then daily: `git push` to send commits up, `git pull` to bring others' down, `git clone ` to copy an existing repo. ##### Pull requests A **pull request** proposes merging a branch: "here are my commits — please review." It is the unit of collaboration in professional teams, and it gives you a place for discussion, review comments and automated checks before code reaches `main`. ```bash git switch -c fix/data-leakage # ... commit your work ... git push -u origin fix/data-leakage gh pr create --title "fix: stratify split to prevent class leakage" \ --body "Test set had no minority-class examples. Adds stratify=y." ``` Even working alone, PRs are worth using. They force you to read your own diff before merging, which catches a remarkable number of mistakes — including committed secrets and stray debugging code. ##### READMEs For an AI engineer, the README is the difference between a repository someone evaluates and one they close. Recruiters and hiring managers look at README files. ```markdown # Customer Churn Predictor Predicts which customers are likely to cancel, using a Random Forest on account activity data. **ROC-AUC 0.89** on a held-out test set (n=4,000). ## Problem A subscription business loses ~8% of customers monthly with no early warning. This model flags at-risk accounts 30 days ahead so retention can intervene. ## Results | Model | Accuracy | Precision | Recall | ROC-AUC | |---|---|---|---|---| | Logistic Regression (baseline) | 0.78 | 0.61 | 0.54 | 0.81 | | Random Forest | 0.84 | 0.72 | 0.68 | 0.89 | ## Quickstart ```bash python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt python src/train.py --data data/customers.csv ``` ## Project structure ``` src/ training and inference code notebooks/ exploratory analysis tests/ pytest suite ``` ## What I'd improve Class imbalance handling (SMOTE), and a proper time-based split — the current random split slightly overstates performance for a temporal problem. ``` Notice what it leads with: **the problem and the result**, not the technology. The "what I'd improve" section signals that you evaluate your own work, which reads as maturity rather than weakness. ##### Why committed keys are dangerous Worth stating plainly, because AI projects involve API keys constantly. **Git history is permanent by default.** Commit an OpenAI key, delete it in the next commit, and it is still in the history — visible in `git log -p`, and present in every clone anyone has made. Removing it properly requires rewriting history and force-pushing. Meanwhile, automated scanners crawl public GitHub continuously. Leaked keys are typically exploited within minutes, and there are well-documented cases of large bills accrued overnight. So: write `.gitignore` **before** creating `.env`; run `git status` and actually read the file list before every commit; commit a `.env.example` with variable names and empty values; enable GitHub's secret scanning and push protection. And if you do leak a key, **revoke and rotate it immediately** — that is the real fix, because the key is already compromised. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[.gitignore first] --> B[Write code] B --> C[git status
READ the file list] C --> D[git add specific files] D --> E[git commit -m
with the result] E --> F[git push] F --> G{Sharing work?} G -->|yes| H[Branch + PR
review your own diff] G -->|no| B H --> I[Merge to main] ``` ##### Common mistakes - **`git add .` without reading `git status`** — the classic way secrets and 500 MB model files get committed. - **Committing datasets and model weights** — use `.gitignore`, and Git LFS or cloud storage if you must version them. - **Messages like "update" or "fix"** — useless six months later. - **Working only on `main`** for risky experiments. - **Never pushing** — a local-only repository is not a backup. - **`git push --force`** on a shared branch, overwriting others' work. - **Committing notebooks with output** — clear them first, or use `nbstripout`. - **Giant commits** mixing unrelated changes, which cannot be reverted cleanly. - **No README**, which makes a good project invisible. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: **initialize a repo, make several commits on a feature branch, and merge it into `main`, resolving a deliberate conflict**. Create the conflict on purpose — edit the same line on both branches — because the first conflict you resolve should be one you engineered, not one that appears at midnight before a deadline. The mini project is your portfolio foundation: **publish your previous projects to a well-organized GitHub profile with READMEs and a Python `.gitignore`**. Write the README for a stranger who has thirty seconds: what problem it solves, what the result was, how to run it. Those three sections do most of the work. For the assignment, **fork an open-source repo, make a small improvement, and open a pull request** following its contribution guidelines. Start genuinely small — a typo in documentation, a clarified error message, a missing docstring. The point is not the contribution's size; it is completing the full loop of fork, branch, commit, push, PR, and responding to review comments. `firstcontributions/first-contributions` exists precisely for this rehearsal, and doing it once removes the intimidation permanently. ##### Key takeaways - Git records every version with a reason, so experiments become recoverable rather than one-way — essential when your job is trying things that might not work. - The loop is `status` → `add` → `commit` → `push`, with messages that record what changed and what it achieved. - Branch for every experiment so `main` always holds your best working version; merge what helps and delete what does not. - Write `.gitignore` before your first secret or dataset exists, keeping `.env`, data, notebooks' checkpoints and model weights out of the repository. - READMEs and pull requests are portfolio and review tools — lead the README with the problem and the measured result, and review your own diff before merging.
